statement: Eleven coins lie on a table, all heads up. In one move you must turn over exactly three of the coins. What is the least number of moves needed to make all eleven coins show tails?

choices.misconception: I divided 11 by 3 and rounded down.
I divided 11 by 3 and rounded up, without checking whether four moves can actually finish.
I counted one move for every coin that has to end up showing tails.
I thought an odd number of heads could never be cleared three at a time because 11 is not a multiple of 3.

hints: Watch whether the number of heads is odd or even after each move.
Turning three coins changes the number of heads by an odd amount, so its parity flips every move. Combine that parity rule with the most heads a single move can remove.
Each move removes at most 3 heads, so at least 4 moves are needed, and the number of moves must be odd to go from 11 heads to 0.

solutions.reliable: If a move turns over k heads and 3 - k tails, the number of heads changes by 3 - 2k, which is odd. So after an even number of moves the head count is odd, and 0 heads needs an odd number of moves. Each move removes at most 3 heads, so at least 4 moves are needed; the least odd number at least 4 is 5. Five moves work: three moves of three heads leave 2 heads; turn one head and two tails to get 3 heads; turn those 3. The transferable idea: combine a parity invariant with a simple bound, then build an example to show the bound is reached.

whyOnTest: Parity of a count that changes by an odd amount each move is a classic 5-point tool, and it overturns the obvious division estimate.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
